title: Kierkegaard
summary: Søren Kierkegaard was a Danish thinker often called the father of existentialism. He was interested not in abstract systems but in the living, single individual who must make a choice and become themselves. He wrote about anxiety, despair and faith as the central events of inner life.
onEmotions: For Kierkegaard, heavy feelings are not obstacles but signposts: anxiety shows that you are free, despair that you have not yet fully become yourself. He believed they can't simply be removed — they have to be passed through, accepted as part of the self's becoming. He described three “stages of existence”: the aesthetic (life for the sake of impressions), the ethical (a life of choice and responsibility) and the religious (a personal relationship to the infinite). Each stage colors experience in its own way, and the transition between them often happens through a crisis — through a “leap,” a decision that can't be calculated in advance.

anxiety.text: Picture someone at a cliff's edge: what frightens him is not only the drop but his freedom to step into it. Kierkegaard built one of the most precise books on anxiety around this image — and if uncertainty is making your head spin, he would understand. In The Concept of Anxiety (the Danish word Angest is translated both as “dread” and as “anxiety”), he wrote that anxiety arises in the face of possibility. When a person looks into an open future where they could choose either this or that, their head spins, like someone looking down from a great height. Hence his famous image: anxiety is “the dizziness of freedom.” So anxiety isn't a sign that you're weak but a sign that you're free and your life isn't predetermined. Kierkegaard even believed that whoever has learned to be anxious in the right way has learned the most important thing. Anxiety is a school: through it we learn that our life is in our own hands.
anxiety.practice: Stand up, feel the floor under your feet and silently name one possibility that is making your “head spin” right now. Tell it, “You are a sign of my freedom,” and take one slow out-breath.

quote.text: Anxiety is the dizziness of freedom.
quote.author: Søren Kierkegaard

fear.text: Abraham walked for three days toward Mount Moriah without knowing how the journey would end — Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling is built entirely around those three days. There's nothing shameful in being afraid: even the knight of faith walked trembling. Kierkegaard drew an important distinction: fear in the narrow sense is always directed at something definite — an event, a person, a danger. Anxiety, by contrast, is directed at “nothing,” at an indefinite possibility. It follows that fear has an advantage: it has an object, it can be named. Sometimes it helps to ask yourself what exactly you're afraid of — and often behind a concrete fear lies a deeper anxiety about yourself and your choice. In Fear and Trembling, Kierkegaard wrote of faith as the resolve to act without guarantees. Following him, courage can be understood this way: not the absence of fear, but a step taken together with it.
fear.practice: Walk slowly — even just across the room — as if on a small “road to Moriah”: with each step, silently name what exactly you're afraid of. By the end of the walk, notice which word turned out to matter most.

sadness.text: “Heaviness of mind” is the literal meaning of the Danish Tungsind, the word Kierkegaard used all his life for his own melancholy. If you are sad right now, he would never demand cheerfulness from you. He didn't consider it simply a bad mood. In the second volume of Either/Or, his character Judge William says that melancholy is a sign that the spirit wants to break through: a person must “choose himself” rather than dissolve into diversions. In other words, sadness may be not a malfunction but a question life is asking you personally: are you living the way you really want to? Kierkegaard didn't rush the answer. What matters is not to run from this question into busyness but to let it be heard — sadness has its own time.
sadness.practice: Sit by a window and let your sadness ask its question: “Are you living the way you really want to?” Don't answer right away — just hold the question in silence for a minute or two.

grief.text: By the age of twenty-five Kierkegaard had buried his mother, his father and five of his six brothers and sisters — his father believed a curse lay on the family. Grief needs time, and no one has the right to hurry it. His thought is steeped in this experience. In Works of Love there's a reflection on love for the dead as the most unselfish and faithful form of love: the one who is gone can give nothing back, and so remembering them is a pure gift. Think this through, and grief is love that continues when there's nowhere left to direct it. Kierkegaard called recollecting the dead one of the “works of love.” And there's a support to be found in this: your pain isn't only a loss but also faithfulness. To live through it is to go on loving.
grief.practice: Do one small “work of love” for the one who is gone, as Kierkegaard called it: say their name aloud, tell someone one story about them, or gently rearrange something of theirs.

loneliness.text: Kierkegaard spent hours every day wandering Copenhagen and chatting with whoever he met — and yet he was perhaps the loneliest man in the city. If you feel lonely right now, there is nothing shameful in that weight. Kierkegaard, however, gave enormous importance to the idea of “the single individual” (den Enkelte) — the separate person who faces life on their own rather than dissolving into the “crowd” or the “public.” He criticized the crowd for relieving people of responsibility and making them faceless. Then loneliness holds not only pain but also a place where you meet yourself. This doesn't mean you should live without people: in Works of Love, Kierkegaard insisted on love of the neighbor. But real closeness, in his view, is possible between those who remain themselves rather than dissolving into others. Loneliness can be the beginning of such closeness.
loneliness.practice: Do what Kierkegaard did on the streets of Copenhagen: go out and exchange a few words with someone you don't know or barely know — a shop assistant, a neighbour. Notice that you remain yourself even in this short conversation.

quote.author: Søren Kierkegaard
quote.source: “That Single Individual,” appendix to The Point of View for My Work as an Author (publ. 1859)

anger.text: As a boy herding sheep on the Jutland heath, Kierkegaard's father, hungry and frozen, once climbed a hill and cursed God; his son believed that rage had marked the whole family. Behind anger there is almost always a wounded value, and there is nothing shameful in it. Kierkegaard wrote little about anger directly, but his ideas help us see it differently. In his treatise on despair (1849), he described various forms of a person's wrong relationship to themselves. One of them is “defiance” — the despairing wish to be yourself in spite of everything, a rebellion against a life that isn't the way we need it to be. This means behind strong anger there is sometimes exactly this: pain that the world doesn't obey our idea of ourselves. Kierkegaard saw in such rebellion a strength of spirit, not a vice. The only question is where to direct it: against life, or toward becoming more honestly yourself.
anger.practice: Find a place where you can stand up to your full height and ask yourself aloud: “Am I angry at this act — or at the fact that life isn't the way I demand?” Hear the answer before you act.

shame.text: “The crowd is untruth,” Kierkegaard wrote, and this short phrase became one of his best known. When shame burns, it feels as if you're being seen right through and found lacking. Kierkegaard wrote a lot about how people live looking over their shoulder at “the others,” afraid of being separate. In his treatise on despair he describes a person who, seeing how everyone else lives, finds it too risky to be himself and becomes a “copy,” worn smooth like a coin in circulation. In Kierkegaard's terms, shame is often born from an outside gaze: we measure ourselves by the yardstick of other people's expectations. Kierkegaard proposed a different point of reference — to stand before yourself (and for him, before God) as a single, unrepeatable person. Before such a gaze you can't be a “not good enough copy,” because you aren't a copy.
shame.practice: Imagine you are standing not before a crowd but before one single attentive and kind gaze. What does that gaze see in you right now? Stay under it for a minute.

guilt.text: All his life Kierkegaard carried guilt for breaking off his engagement to Regine Olsen, and in his will he left her everything he owned. He knew guilt from the inside and never simplified it. He linked the capacity to feel guilt with freedom: only someone who could have acted otherwise can feel guilty. In The Concept of Anxiety he shows how closely anxiety and guilt are intertwined: anxiety precedes a free act, and guilt accompanies it. But Kierkegaard was also a thinker of forgiveness. In his religious works, forgiveness isn't forgetting but a new beginning. In Repetition he speaks of the possibility of receiving life anew without denying the past. Seen this way, guilt isn't the end of the story but a place from which honest renewal can begin. You can acknowledge it without turning it into a verdict on yourself.
guilt.practice: Write yourself a short note under a pseudonym, as Kierkegaard did — say, “The Witness.” Let this witness name honestly what happened and add one step from which renewal could begin.

envy.text: Copenhagen's public in the 1840s carried some writers shoulder-high and ignored others, and Kierkegaard knew well what it is to watch someone else's success from the side. Envy is unpleasant, and many people are ashamed of it. Kierkegaard offered an unexpected view: in his treatise on despair he wrote that envy is secret admiration. The one who envies is really admiring, but doesn't dare admit it to themselves and turns admiration into resentment. And in A Literary Review (1846) he described “leveling” — the mood of an age when envy becomes a way of trimming everyone down to one measure so that no one stands out. In this light, your envy can be a signpost: it shows what truly fills you with admiration and what you'd like to develop in yourself. Rather than suppressing envy, you can “decode” it — and give it back its original meaning of admiration.
envy.practice: Turn your envy into admiration aloud: say — to yourself or straight to this person — “What I admire in you is…”. Then choose one tiny thing you can do today to nurture that in yourself.

emptiness.text: The greatest danger, losing one's self, can happen very quietly, as if it were nothing at all, Kierkegaard warned. Emptiness and apathy are very heavy, and there's no need to blame yourself for them. In his treatise on despair (1849), Kierkegaard describes despair not as a stormy drama but often as a quiet, unnoticed state: a person lives, works, socializes — but as if not present in their own life, not being themselves. He even noted that the most common despair is the kind that doesn't know it is despair. So the feeling of emptiness may not be empty at all: it's a signal that your self is asking for attention. For Kierkegaard, the way out of despair is to dare to “be yourself,” to establish an honest relationship with yourself. This doesn't happen in a moment; it's a path of small honest steps, and the first of them is noticing that you feel empty.
emptiness.practice: Recall when in the past week you were closest to yourself — and repeat even a tiny part of that moment today: the same music, the same road, the same person.

confusion.text: In Gribskov forest north of Copenhagen, Kierkegaard loved a spot where eight roads meet — in his words, the right place for solitude and reflection. Confusion is standing at such a crossroads, not knowing where to go or who to be. Kierkegaard knew this state well: he himself agonized over choosing his path — in love, in his vocation. He believed that life can't be derived from a system like a theorem: no philosophy will make the decision for you. Hence his idea of the “leap”: you pass to a new way of life not through endless reasoning but through a decision that always carries risk. It follows that confusion is a natural pause before a choice, not a sign of your inability. Kierkegaard also offers the comfort that the meaning of the road traveled often becomes visible only later. Right now you may not understand where you're going — and still walk on.
confusion.practice: Take one step forward — literally, right there in the room — and name aloud the smallest step in your life you could take without knowing the whole road. Kierkegaard would call it a tiny “leap.”

quote.text: Life can only be understood backwards; but it must be lived forwards.
quote.author: Søren Kierkegaard

fatigue.text: Kierkegaard kept some fifty cups, and each morning his secretary had to pick one and say why. Even a man who wrote dozens of books in a few years kept this tiny, unhurried ceremony. If your strength is now smaller than the demands, that's an honest signal. Kierkegaard wrote ironically about people so absorbed in their affairs that they have no time to be themselves. He considered bustle and “busyness” one of the ways of running away from yourself: as long as we're busy, we don't have to ask ourselves the main questions. In other words, burnout happens when we live for a long time for the sake of external tasks, forgetting the inner. Kierkegaard reminded us that the self isn't a role or a function but a person's relationship to themselves. Rest, then, isn't idleness but a return to that relationship: to a silence in which your own voice can be heard again. You don't have to earn such rest.
fatigue.practice: Hold your own “cup ceremony,” as Kierkegaard did: choose a cup, explain to yourself why this one, and drink your tea or water slowly, doing nothing else.

boredom.text: “The gods were bored, so they created man”: this is how Kierkegaard's aesthete begins his history of the world in the essay “Crop Rotation” in Either/Or. Boredom may seem trivial, but Kierkegaard devoted a whole essay to it. His aesthete hero claims that boredom is the root of all evil and proposes a clever “rotation of crops”: not changing fields, but changing the way you look at the same thing, playing with impressions. But Kierkegaard shows that this is still a trap of the “aesthetic stage”: a life lived for what's interesting sooner or later exhausts itself. Think this through, and boredom is a signal that the chase after impressions no longer nourishes you. The way out, for Kierkegaard, lies not in new stimuli but in the transition to the “ethical” stage: to choice, commitment, something you are responsible for. Boredom can be a door, not a dead end.
boredom.practice: Try the aesthete's “crop rotation,” but honestly: for a minute look at one familiar thing in the room as if you were seeing it for the first time. Then ask yourself what small thing in your life you're ready to answer for — not because it's interesting, but because it matters.

joy.text: The lily does nothing to be a lily, and the bird stores no grain for tomorrow — these are exactly the ones Kierkegaard called teachers of joy. You can accept your joy without justifying it. Kierkegaard, known as a thinker of anxiety, also wrote beautiful pages about joy — in the discourses The Lily in the Field and the Bird of the Air (1849). He asks what we can learn from the lily and the bird, and one of his discourses answers: joy. In his view, joy means being truly in the present, “today,” not handing yourself over entirely to tomorrow's worries. The lily and the bird don't worry about tomorrow — that's why they are joyful. Then joy doesn't need to be earned or saved up: it opens when you are here, wholly, in this moment. Kierkegaard believed such joy can be found even in the midst of difficulties.
joy.practice: Find a bird, a tree or a flower outside the window or on the street and watch for a minute how it simply is, “today.” Tell yourself, “Now — today,” and let the joy be, without a reason.

love.text: Six years after breaking with Regine, Kierkegaard wrote Works of Love (1847) — one of the deepest books about what it means to love. The tenderness you feel now he considered the most precious thing in a person. He distinguished “preferential” love — for those especially dear to us — from love of the “neighbor,” directed at every person. One of his main ideas: love “builds up,” that is, it presupposes love in the other and thereby helps it grow. The one who loves sees more good in another than that person sees in themselves. This means your tenderness isn't naivety but a creative force: it doesn't just reflect the world, it changes it. Kierkegaard also wrote that love is known by its fruits — by deeds, not only by feelings. Tenderness asks for small acts.
love.practice: Love, for Kierkegaard, “builds up”: it presupposes good in the other and helps it grow. Today, tell someone you love one good thing you see in them — perhaps more clearly than they do.

gratitude.text: Kierkegaard dedicated his Upbuilding Discourses to his father and addressed them to “that single individual whom with joy and gratitude I call my reader.” He considered the warm feeling of gratitude something very deep. Several of his Upbuilding Discourses (1843) are devoted to a line from the Epistle of James: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above.” He reflects on how hard it can be to give thanks when life doesn't match our expectations, and on how gratitude changes the one who gives thanks. In Kierkegaard's terms, gratitude isn't a polite formality but a way of relating to life: you stop only demanding from it and begin to receive. You needn't share Kierkegaard's religious views to take this thought from him: gratitude is an inner movement in which a person becomes gentler and freer.
gratitude.practice: Read aloud the line Kierkegaard reflected on — “Every good gift…” — or one of your own that is closer to you. Then name three gifts of this day that you didn't earn and didn't plan.

hope.text: Kierkegaard was convinced that no one has the right to put a full stop after a human being — neither after another nor after oneself. Hope helps us go on living, and he valued it very highly. In his treatise on despair he wrote that what a person in despair needs above all is “possibility” — the sense that not everything is settled; without it, it's as if there were no air to breathe. For him this was connected with faith: “for God all things are possible.” In Works of Love he adds that love “hopes all things,” meaning that hope is also an attitude toward another person: not writing them off, leaving them a future. Seen this way, hope isn't naive optimism but a decision to keep possibility open, even when you can't see it. You can apply this to yourself too: not passing a final verdict on yourself, leaving yourself a future.
hope.practice: Say aloud, “It's still possible that…” — about yourself or someone close — and finish it. Kierkegaard would call it a breath of air; just breathe it for a minute.

nostalgia.text: Hope is a new garment, recollection a discarded one you've outgrown, and repetition a garment that never wears out: this is how Kierkegaard opens his book Repetition. Longing for the past is tender, and you can live it gently. Kierkegaard thought a lot about memory. In Repetition (1843) he contrasted “recollection” and “repetition.” Recollection faces backward: it preserves what is lost, and so it is tinged with sadness. Repetition faces forward: it is the capacity to receive what is precious again — not copying the past, but living its meaning anew. And in Either/Or there's an essay on “the unhappiest one” — a person who lives only in recollection or only in expectation and is never present in the present. In this light, nostalgia is beautiful as long as it doesn't take your “today” away from you. You can ask yourself: what of what I long for could be not brought back, but received anew?
nostalgia.practice: Choose one memory you miss and find its heart — not the scenery, but the meaning. Today, do one small thing in which that meaning can be “repeated” in a new form.

craving.text: Kierkegaard knew how “now or never” sounds inside: his “Seducer's Diary” is a whole book about a man who lives from one desire to the next. A sharp “I want it right now” doesn't make you a bad person. Kierkegaard described a similar life under the name of the “aesthetic stage” — a life ruled by immediate desires and moods. His aesthete hero in the first volume of Either/Or admits himself that pleasure disappoints, while possibility does not. So a craving promises not so much a substance or a thing as the feeling that everything is about to be different. Kierkegaard saw the way out not in prohibition but in choice: in a person one day choosing themselves — not their desire, but the self who is experiencing that desire. A craving says “now or never.” But between the wave and the act there is always a moment, and in it, you live.
craving.practice: When a craving washes over you, tell yourself, “I notice the desire, and I am the one who notices it.” Wait three slow breaths before doing anything — this is Kierkegaard's moment between the wave and the act.

addiction.text: “Purity of Heart Is to Will One Thing” is the title of one of Kierkegaard's best-known discourses, and anyone long caught in the circle of addiction knows how hard it is to hold on to that one thing. This circle is hard to leave, and that isn't a moral failure. Kierkegaard would say that addiction touches the deepest part of a person — their self. In his treatise on despair he defines the self as a relation that relates itself to itself. It follows that in addiction this relation seems to pass over to something else: life becomes organized around a substance or a habit, and the person themselves is pushed aside. Kierkegaard also wrote about “purity of heart” — being able to will one thing rather than being torn apart. But he never thought a person manages this alone or all at once. For him, the path to oneself always passed through honesty, through a willingness to admit one's need and accept help.
addiction.practice: Tell one person you trust one honest sentence about how you are right now. Kierkegaard believed the path to oneself begins with admitting one's need; if you like, you can say that sentence in a mutual-help group too.

hangover.text: Judge William, the soberest voice in Kierkegaard, says a person must “choose himself” — not the best version, but the whole self, yesterday included. This morning, when your body aches and anxiety, shame and gaps in memory pile on, there's no need to finish yourself off. Kierkegaard clearly distinguished two ways of relating to your past. You can judge yourself endlessly — and then, in his view, a person despairs not only over the act but over themselves, and the despair becomes double. Or you can do what Judge William in the second volume of Either/Or calls “choosing yourself”: acknowledging your history as your own, neither disowning it nor drowning in it. In other words, morning shame is a signal that you care. You don't need to settle everything today. It's enough to say to yourself honestly: “This happened to me, and I am here.”
hangover.practice: Take care of your body: water, fresh air. Then, as Judge William advises, “choose yourself” aloud: “Yesterday happened to me, and I am here. Today I take one kind step,” — and name that step.

euphoria.text: When Either/Or came out, all of Copenhagen guessed at who was hiding behind the pseudonym Victor Eremita, while the author quietly savoured his success. A bright surge when everything seems possible is something you can be glad of. Kierkegaard understood this light well: his aesthete in Either/Or confesses that he would wish for himself not wealth or power but the passion for the possible — an eye that sees possibility everywhere. For Kierkegaard, “possibility” isn't an empty dream but one of the two sides of the self: a person is woven from the possible and the necessary, from flight and ground. Think this through, and euphoria is a moment when the side of the possible suddenly shines at full strength. There's no need to put it out. Kierkegaard would suggest just one thing: so that the flash doesn't fly away entirely, tie it to something small and real. Then possibility becomes not only a feeling but part of your life.
euphoria.practice: Touch the possibility today: take one very small action toward it — a message, a call, the first five minutes of the task. Kierkegaard would say this is how the passion for the possible becomes part of actuality.

crash.text: In the evening, lights and laughter; in the morning, an empty hall — Kierkegaard knew such swings so well that he made a plot out of them. If you've been thrown down sharply after a high, it can be very hard. Kierkegaard wrote a whole book about this — Repetition (1843). Its narrator, Constantin Constantius, once had a wonderful time in Berlin and decided to go back to repeat it all. But nothing worked: the room wasn't right, the theater gave no pleasure, everything seemed faded. Then a slump is often born from trying to hold on to or repeat the high. Kierkegaard distinguished this kind of repetition from the real one: when life isn't brought back by force but received anew, as a gift — in a new form. Right now you don't need to bring anything back. You can simply let yourself come down and wait for what comes.
crash.practice: Tell yourself, “I don't need to repeat yesterday's high.” Go for a short walk and find one small good thing on the way, nothing like that high — let it be your new “repetition.”

panic.text: Kierkegaard, who wrote all his life about fear and trembling, would never tell you to “just calm down”: your heart is pounding, you can't get enough air, and this is genuinely hard right now. In The Concept of Anxiety Kierkegaard offered an image that helps many people: someone who looks down into a yawning abyss grows dizzy, and the cause, he wrote, lies not only in the abyss but also in the eye that looks into it. This means panic, too, pulls your gaze into the abyss — toward the worst thing that could happen. Such a wave usually rises, peaks and subsides within a few minutes. And when you're dizzy, something simple helps: shifting your gaze to what is near and solid, and holding on to what you can touch.
panic.practice: Take your eyes off the “abyss”: put your feet on the floor, lay your palm on something solid and breathe out for longer than you breathe in. Name five objects right beside you — things you can touch.

dread.text: In the summer of 1835 the twenty-two-year-old Kierkegaard wandered the shore near the fishing village of Gilleleje, tormented by the question of what to live for. “What is all this for,” thoughts of finitude and the abyss — this is one of the heaviest experiences, and he knew it from the inside. Back then he wrote in his journal that he needed to find a truth that was true for him, an idea for which he wanted to live. Not a general system, but his own meaning. And in the discourse “At a Graveside” (1845) he wrote that the thought of finitude can teach “earnestness”: it makes today precious and keeps you from putting off what matters most. In Kierkegaard's terms, your dread isn't a sign that there's no meaning, but the beginning of your own question about meaning. Such a question isn't answered in one night. You carry it within you, and little by little it begins to change how you live today.
dread.practice: Go where you can see far — to a window, a balcony, the street — and, like Kierkegaard on the shore at Gilleleje, ask yourself: what truly matters to me today? Let the answer be very small.

fomo.text: Wherever Kierkegaard's aesthete is, real life seems to be happening somewhere else. Feeling that everyone lives more interesting lives and you're in the wrong place is very draining. Kierkegaard described it with astonishing precision. In the first volume of Either/Or there's an “ecstatic lecture”: marry, and you'll regret it; don't marry, and you'll regret that too; do it, and you'll regret it; don't, and you'll regret it. And in the essay on “the unhappiest one” he paints a person who is never present in their own life: they live now in hope of the future, now in memory of the past. Seen this way, the fear of missing out is a life lived “outside yourself,” in other people's places and possibilities. Kierkegaard's answer is choice: Judge William says that what matters is not so much the right option as the act of choosing itself, in which a person becomes themselves. Where you are is where your life begins.
fomo.practice: Tell yourself aloud, “I choose to be here.” Name one thing that exists only in your today — and stay with it for a minute.

sleepless.text: Why does everything seem huge and unsolvable at three in the morning? Kierkegaard would answer: because at night we live in a tomorrow that doesn't exist yet. You're not alone in this. In Christian Discourses (1848), Kierkegaard devoted a separate reflection to worry about tomorrow and called it “the worry of self-torment.” He wrote that the bird of the air doesn't know this worry, because it has no “tomorrow” — only “today.” In this light, night thoughts are almost always about tomorrow: about what hasn't happened yet and what nothing can be done about right now. Kierkegaard would suggest not fighting these thoughts but gently bringing yourself back to “today” — to this room, this breath, this moment, in which there are no tomorrow's tasks.
sleepless.practice: Tell yourself, “Tomorrow's things are for tomorrow.” Put your palm on your chest and count ten slow out-breaths, like the bird that has only “today.”

betrayal.text: “Love believes all things — and yet is never deceived”: Kierkegaard examines this paradox in Works of Love. When you are betrayed, what collapses is not only a relationship but your faith in your own trust, and the pain of that is justified. He reflected on what to do with trust after being deceived. He noted that mistrust can be a self-deception too: it seems wise, but in fact it simply chooses the worst explanation. And he voiced a bold thought: whoever deceives the one who loves ultimately deceives themselves most of all, depriving themselves of what is most precious. So your trust wasn't foolishness — it was your capacity to love, and it still belongs to you. You don't have to forgive anyone on a schedule. But you can refuse to let this wound take you away from yourself.
betrayal.practice: Say aloud, “My trust says about me that I…” — and finish it. Name one quality you want to keep despite what happened.

jealousy.text: Kierkegaard kept watching Regine's life jealously even after the break: on learning of her engagement to Schlegel, he tore whole pages out of a manuscript. Burning jealousy is nothing to be ashamed of: it shows how much another person means to you. In Works of Love, Kierkegaard distinguished “preferential” love — for those especially dear to us — from love of the “neighbor.” He wrote of the first with great respect, but honestly noted its vulnerability: immediate love can change within itself and turn into jealousy. It follows that jealousy is love seized by the fear of loss. Kierkegaard didn't demand giving it up, but suggested adding a second dimension to love: seeing the beloved not only as “my” person but also as a separate, free individual. This doesn't extinguish the feeling, but it gives it more air.
jealousy.practice: Picture the person you love at a moment when they're busy with something of their own, without you, and name one quality that belongs only to them. Notice what happens to the jealousy when you see a separate, free person.

resentment.text: To the end of his life Kierkegaard did not forgive the Danish Church and Bishop Mynster for what he saw as falseness, and in his last year he put out angry pamphlets called The Moment. A long-held grudge is a heavy load, and behind it there is almost always a real injustice. In his treatise on despair, Kierkegaard described a striking state: a person has grown so attached to their pain that they can no longer give it up, because it has become part of them, proof that they were right. In other words, resentment sometimes holds on to us not because we want to suffer, but because parting with it feels like a betrayal of ourselves. Kierkegaard didn't demand hasty forgiveness. He suggested seeing that the self is larger than any wound: it can acknowledge the wound — and still not live only for it. Letting go begins not with forgetting but with a question: who would I be without this weight?
resentment.practice: Ask yourself aloud, “Who would I be without this weight?” Don't answer right away — just hold the question for a minute, the way Kierkegaard held his questions without rushing to settle them.

heartbreak.text: Kierkegaard returned Regine Olsen's ring with a letter asking her above all to “forget the one who writes this” — and he himself never forgot her. A broken heart is one of the sharpest pains, and no one has the right to hurry it. Kierkegaard lived through it himself: this was in 1841, and according to his own journals he thought about Regine all his life. This wound runs through many of his books. In Repetition, a young man going through a love drama writes long letters and suffers, not knowing how to go on living. Kierkegaard shows that it is possible to get through such pain — not by trying to bring back the past, but through life being given back little by little, in a new form. Think this through, and your grief isn't an end but part of your self's becoming. For now, it's enough simply to allow yourself to grieve.
heartbreak.practice: Write a short farewell letter to this love that you won't send, and sign it with a pseudonym, as Kierkegaard did. Then put it aside — let it rest.

impostor.text: Johannes Climacus, Victor Eremita, Johannes de Silentio, Anti-Climacus — Kierkegaard signed his books with so many names that readers wondered where he himself was. The feeling that you're about to be exposed especially often visits conscientious people. He himself pondered where the real author was behind these masks. But above all, he criticized “the public,” the faceless crowd whose judgments we submit to, although it is, in his words, an abstraction, a phantom. What mattered most to him was “the single individual” — a person who stands before life (for Kierkegaard, before God) on their own, not before an audience. Then the impostor is a role we play for imaginary spectators. Before yourself you aren't an “impostor” but a person on the way, learning and growing.
impostor.practice: Imagine the auditorium is empty and the lights are off. Right now, do one thing you can do and love doing — for yourself, not for an audience — and notice who is doing it.

self_hatred.text: Anti-Climacus is the strictest of Kierkegaard's pseudonyms, and even he calls the despairing unwillingness to be oneself a sickness, not a crime. Your inner critic is causing enormous pain right now, and you don't deserve that verdict. In his treatise on despair, Kierkegaard described a form of suffering in which a person despairingly does not want to be themselves and would like to be rid of themselves. He saw in this not a vice but a sickness of the self, which calls for gentleness, not fresh reproaches. And in Works of Love he has a striking thought: the commandment “love your neighbor as yourself” presupposes that the right love of oneself and love of one's neighbor are, at heart, one and the same. This means the inner critic violates not only your peace but the very nature of love. Loving yourself in the right way isn't selfishness but part of knowing how to love.
self_hatred.practice: Think of someone you sincerely love and say one sentence to yourself aloud, in the same tone you would use with them. Kierkegaard would call it the right love of oneself — the kind contained in the commandment itself.

helplessness.text: “To Need God Is a Human Being's Highest Perfection”: the title of one of Kierkegaard's discourses sounds almost like a challenge to everyone who teaches us to rely only on ourselves. If it feels as though you can't change anything, that is not your fault. He wrote this discourse in 1844. He wrote that admitting you can do little on your own isn't a defeat but the beginning of a genuine relationship to life. For Kierkegaard this was a religious path. But even outside faith, his thought can be read this way: powerlessness lays bare the fact that human beings aren't made to cope alone. So what matters now is not pretending you're all-powerful, but allowing yourself to need others — help, support, someone else's presence beside you.
helplessness.practice: Call or message one person and ask for something small — advice, help, just to be near. Kierkegaard would say that by admitting your need you haven't lost; you've begun.

procrastination.text: Kierkegaard wrote Either/Or — nearly nine hundred pages — in less than a year, yet his aesthete can't make himself get up off the sofa. The “I can't get started” state is exhausting, and it doesn't mean you're lazy. Kierkegaard described it in the “Diapsalmata” — the aesthete's aphorisms in the first volume of Either/Or. The aesthete complains: riding is too violent, walking too tiring; lie down — and then you'll have to either stay lying down or get up again, and he wants neither. He doesn't feel like anything. Seen this way, procrastination is life among endless possibilities, none of which has been chosen. Kierkegaard believed that no amount of preparation cancels the “leap”: a decision that can't be calculated in advance can only be made. The leap doesn't have to be huge. Sometimes it's simply the first movement of your hand toward the task.
procrastination.practice: Make a small “leap” literally: stand up, say aloud, “I'm starting,” and do the first two-minute step of the task at once. Only that — you can stop after it.

uprooted.text: Kierkegaard went to Berlin four times, and each time he came back to Copenhagen with a new book. Being cut off from home — a move, emigration — is a hard experience, as if the ground were slipping from under your feet. Kierkegaard lived almost his whole life in Copenhagen, but in his most difficult period — after breaking off his engagement — he went to Berlin, and there he wrote most of Either/Or. Far from home, he was looking not for a new place but for himself. For Kierkegaard, the self isn't a place or a setting but a person's relationship to themselves, which they can build anew anywhere. In this light, moving takes away outer supports but leaves the main one — your capacity to become yourself. Homesickness is legitimate. But in a new place, too, there's something no one can take from you: your own path.
uprooted.practice: Walk down your new street the way Kierkegaard wandered through foreign Berlin — slowly, noticing details. Find one thing that could become “yours” here: a bench, a tree, a view.

overload.text: “Our age is essentially one of reflection, without passion,” Kierkegaard wrote of the era of newspapers and endless chatter. Overload and the endless feed really are tiring. Kierkegaard, surprisingly, described it almost two hundred years ago. In A Literary Review (1846) he speaks of “the present age” as an age of reflection and chatter: everyone discusses everything, the press creates “the public,” and the individual dissolves into an endless exchange of opinions and puts off living their own life. So overload isn't only fatigue from information but also the loss of your own voice. Kierkegaard knew a simple remedy: he walked around Copenhagen almost every day and considered walks the source of his best thoughts. Sometimes the only answer to noise is to step out of it, even briefly.
overload.practice: Go outside for five minutes without your phone and just walk, as Kierkegaard did in Copenhagen. If you can't go out, close your eyes and listen to the sounds around you without naming them.

quote.text: I know of no thought so burdensome that one cannot walk away from it.
quote.author: Søren Kierkegaard

unreality.text: What do you do when your own life seems like a play watched from a distant box? Kierkegaard knew this too. The feeling that nothing is real can be very frightening, and it's hard to tell others about. In his dissertation On the Concept of Irony (1841) he portrayed a person for whom all of actuality has “lost its validity” — everything has become distant, as if on a stage. And in his treatise on despair he wrote of the “despair of infinitude,” when the self seems to evaporate into fantasy and loses touch with the concrete. It follows that the feeling of unreality isn't your fault and isn't emptiness, but a sign that your connection to the concrete has weakened for a while. Kierkegaard saw the way back in simple things: in small, everyday actions that return a person to the “here.”
unreality.practice: Do one concrete thing with your hands: wash a cup, stroke a piece of fabric. Notice temperature and texture and name them to yourself — Kierkegaard would call it returning from the infinite to the concrete.

awe.text: Kierkegaard took the title Fear and Trembling from Paul's epistle, and the word “trembling” was almost sacred to him. Before something vast or beautiful you want to fall silent — a rare and precious experience. In the discourses The Lily in the Field and the Bird of the Air (1849) he wrote that the first thing the lily and the bird teach is silence. Before the grandeur of the world, a person usually tries to say something, explain it, remember it. But the lily and the bird simply are — and there is more reverence in their silence than in all our words. For Kierkegaard, such silence was a relationship to God; but his thought can be read more broadly too: awe is a moment when words are superfluous. In other words, the best way to live through awe is not to hurry to describe it, photograph it or share it, but simply to be in it.
awe.practice: Spend a minute in silence before whatever filled you with awe — as, for Kierkegaard, the lily and the bird teach. Don't describe it, even to yourself; just look.

relief.text: Kierkegaard loved carriage rides through Zealand: after weeks of work he would race out to the sea and the forest and come back renewed. Relief is a quiet warmth after long tension, and it's worth savouring. Kierkegaard described it in Repetition (1843). The young man in this book suffers for a long time in an unresolvable situation, and when it unexpectedly resolves, he writes a simple sentence: he has become himself again. For Kierkegaard this was true “repetition” — not the return of the past, but receiving yourself anew, as a gift. Think this through, and relief isn't just the disappearance of a weight but a moment when you come back to yourself again. You don't need to rush to fill the freed-up space. Let yourself feel what it's like to be yourself again.
relief.practice: Breathe out slowly and say to yourself, in the words of the young man in Repetition, “I am myself again.” Notice where in your body this resonates.

calm.text: What does a person look like who is at peace inside? Kierkegaard's answer was unexpected: completely ordinary. Calm and peace are a state in which it's good simply to be. Kierkegaard drew a picture of such calm in Fear and Trembling (1843). His “knight of faith” looks nothing like a hero: he looks like an ordinary tax collector, walks the streets, looks forward to his dinner, strolls in the woods and delights in everything he sees. Outwardly there's nothing special about him, but he is fully present in the finite, in ordinary life. For Kierkegaard this calm was the fruit of faith; but his image can be read more broadly too. Then real calm isn't an escape from the world but the ability to be wholly present in the simplest day. Right now, perhaps, this is exactly what you're feeling.
calm.practice: Walk like Kierkegaard's knight of faith — at an ordinary pace down an ordinary street or across a room, enjoying every simple thing: a smell, the light, a sound. Look for nothing — just be in this day.

inspiration.text: Kierkegaard wrote standing at a high desk and produced dozens of books in a few years — sometimes his thought ran faster than his pen. If inspiration has caught you now, it's worth receiving with gratitude. He valued “passion” — not a storm of emotions but a fullness of inner engagement without which, in his view, one can't truly exist. In the Concluding Unscientific Postscript (1846), his pseudonym Johannes Climacus says that for a living person truth isn't an abstraction but the way they live in it. This means inspiration is a moment when thought and life come together. Kierkegaard wouldn't urge you to analyze it. What would matter to him is that it not remain just a mood, but take shape, at least a little, in action.
inspiration.practice: Stand, like Kierkegaard at his desk, and write down what came to you without editing. Then note one small action with which you'll put it into practice in the next few days.

schadenfreude.text: When all Copenhagen laughed at caricatures of Kierkegaard in 1846, he came to know schadenfreude well — from the side of the one being laughed at. Noticing this feeling in yourself is unpleasant: am I really like this? Kierkegaard helps you look at this feeling without self-flagellation. In The Sickness unto Death he wrote that the measure of the self is always that before which it places itself. If we measure ourselves by other people, our sense of self rises and falls with their successes and failures. In Kierkegaard's terms, schadenfreude isn't so much malice as a symptom that you've temporarily started living in someone else's coordinate system: another's fall feels like your rise. Kierkegaard wouldn't shame you. He would ask: before what do I want to be myself? When the measure is your own life and its task, someone else's failure stops meaning anything for your self.
schadenfreude.practice: Ask yourself aloud, as Kierkegaard would: “Before what do I want to be myself right now?” Name your own yardstick — a task, a value, a person — and notice that someone else's failure changes nothing on it.

contempt.text: Socrates, Kierkegaard's favourite hero, claimed to know only that he knew nothing — and so stood level with every passer-by. Contempt is often born of real disappointment in a person. In his dissertation On the Concept of Irony, Kierkegaard wrote about a stance of superiority from which you can look down on everything. He acknowledged its power, but noted that if you make it your permanent point of view, it isolates you — you end up above everyone, and therefore alone. In Works of Love he offered the opposite view: the one who loves “presupposes” the possibility of good in another, even if it can't be seen right now. Contempt, by contrast, sees a person as finished, defined once and for all by their worst act. Seen this way, you don't have to give up your judgment, but you can leave a crack in it for possibility: a person is not only what they have done. And you, too, don't have to live on a cold height.
contempt.practice: Say to yourself, “This person did…, but they are not only that. Perhaps there is also… in them.” Even one word in the second part counts — Kierkegaard would call it love that “presupposes” the good.

disgust.text: Can you look at yourself with disgust and still be closer to healing than someone who is pleased with himself? Kierkegaard answered: yes. Disgust — at a situation, at people or at yourself — is a heavy, repelling feeling. Kierkegaard paid especially close attention to its inward-turned form. In The Sickness unto Death he distinguished despair over something external from despair over oneself, when a person looks at their own weakness with disgust. Unexpectedly, he considered the second a deeper state, and one closer to healing: in it a person at least sees themselves and takes themselves seriously. In this light, disgust with yourself isn't proof of your worthlessness but a sign that you care who you are. Kierkegaard didn't agree with the inner verdict. He suggested taking the next step: accepting this weak self as your own — the only material from which you can go on becoming yourself.
disgust.practice: Step back, take a few slow out-breaths and finish aloud: “What I find disgusting shows that what matters to me is…”. Look at the second half as a signpost, not a verdict.

revenge.text: Who ends up running your day — you, or the one who hurt you? Kierkegaard would ask this uncomfortable question first. The wish for revenge is understandable: you were wronged, and something inside demands justice. In Purity of Heart Is to Will One Thing, Kierkegaard described “double-mindedness” — a state in which a person is torn between different aims and stops being whole. So revenge quietly shifts the center of your life: more and more of your thoughts and strength start to revolve around the person who hurt you, and they, without even meaning to, gain power over you. Kierkegaard didn't demand hasty forgiveness and didn't deny that you were in the right. But he would ask: do I want my self to be defined by this person? You can acknowledge your anger fully — and still put your own life back at the center, your own task, your own “one thing,” not someone else's act.
revenge.practice: Estimate how much of your thinking today this person took up. Choose one activity — your own “one thing,” as Kierkegaard would say — that will give you back a little of your own time, and do it.

anger_at_loved.text: One chapter of Works of Love is called “Our Duty to Love the People We See,” and the whole difficulty of love can be heard in that title. Anger at those close to you is especially hard, because shame follows it. His thought is that we easily love an imagined image — the ideal partner, parent, child — while the real person beside us inevitably fails to match it. It follows that anger often flares where image and reality meet: “they should have been different.” This doesn't mean there's no love — on the contrary, it means your expectations are great. Kierkegaard suggested not giving up love but transferring it from the image to the person as they are. There's no need to shame your anger; you can ask it which image it has just collided with.
anger_at_loved.practice: Look at your loved one — or picture their face — and say to yourself, “Here you are, as you are, not as you should be.” Notice what happens to the anger when the image steps back.

ambivalence.text: Either/Or is what Kierkegaard called his first big book, yet he himself lived his whole life in a “both/and”: he loved Regine and could not be with her. Loving a person and at the same time being unable to stand them is a state you want to be rid of quickly. Kierkegaard knew it from the inside: he loved Regine Olsen, broke off their engagement, and wrote about it all his life, never reducing his feelings to one. His philosophy explains why this isn't a malfunction. In The Sickness unto Death, the self is described as a synthesis of opposites — the finite and the infinite, freedom and necessity — and as a relation that relates itself to itself. In other words, mixed feelings are the natural state of a being woven from contradictions. The task isn't for one feeling to win, but how you yourself relate to both. You can hold them together without rushing to a final decision.
ambivalence.practice: Say one sentence aloud: “I love… and I can't bear…” — joined by “and,” not “but.” Kierkegaard would call it a synthesis; notice what it's like to hold both parts together.

guilty_relief.text: Can a sigh of relief be part of love rather than a betrayal of it? Kierkegaard would say these feelings live on different levels. Relief after a departure, a breakup or the death of a gravely ill loved one often frightens us: was there not enough love? Relief is a response to the end of tension, fear and exhausting caregiving. Love, for Kierkegaard, doesn't end along with circumstances. In Works of Love there's a chapter on the love that remembers one who has died; he called it the most unselfish and the most faithful love, since it receives nothing in return. Think this through, and relief doesn't cancel love: you can breathe out and go on loving, remembering, being grateful. Kierkegaard wouldn't judge you. He would more likely say that your capacity to grieve over your relief itself speaks of the depth of your attachment.
guilty_relief.practice: Do one small “work of the love that remembers”: light a candle, look at a photograph or say a name. Let it live alongside the relief, without arguing with it.

indifference.text: Kierkegaard dreamed of a “single individual” as his reader — not a public with opinions about everything, but a person whom the text would truly touch. When something should move you and doesn't, it's easy to get frightened for yourself. In A Literary Review, Kierkegaard described his age as sensible and passionless: people discuss a lot, know a little about everything, but are rarely truly gripped by anything. He saw this not as a personal vice but as a sickness of the age, where a stream of information replaces living engagement. Then your indifference isn't necessarily callousness. It may be weariness from having to have an opinion and a feeling about everything at once. Kierkegaard valued “inwardness” — what can't be put on show and can't be summoned on command. So there's no point faking a feeling that isn't there. Better to honestly leave room: living engagement comes when a thing becomes yours, not everyone's.
indifference.practice: Ask yourself: is there anything in this situation that concerns me personally, not “everyone”? If you find even one detail — a face, a name, a place — stay with it in silence for a minute.

escape.text: Kierkegaard could have gone anywhere — his father's inheritance allowed it — yet apart from Berlin he hardly ever left Copenhagen. The urge to drop everything — a job, a city, a role — is understandable when life has grown too tight. Kierkegaard described it ironically in the essay “Crop Rotation” in Either/Or. His aesthete hero lists: one person gets tired of living in the country and goes to the city; tired of his homeland, he goes abroad; tired of Europe, he goes to America. Kierkegaard shows that such a change of circumstances often just carries the boredom to a new place. But in the same book Judge William, the voice of the ethical life, proposes another path — “choosing yourself,” that is, taking on your life and its task. This means you can ask: do I want to escape the place, or the way I live in it? Sometimes a change of circumstances is right; sometimes it's choosing yourself within them.
escape.practice: Picture yourself a year from now, there where you want to escape to, and ask, as Judge William would: “Who have I become there?” Find one small step for this new “me” that's possible right here.

forbidden_attraction.text: Why does the unavailable attract more strongly than what's close at hand? Kierkegaard thought about this for years. Attraction to someone unavailable or “wrong” can be embarrassing and unsettling. Kierkegaard wrote a lot about a life drawn toward the possible — in Either/Or this is the world of the aesthete, for whom what's most alluring is not what is but what could be. In The Sickness unto Death he described a self that drifts off into imagined possibilities and loses touch with reality, and a self that clings only to necessity and suffocates. In Kierkegaard's terms, the unavailable attracts partly because it is pure possibility — something untested by reality. Kierkegaard wouldn't pass a verdict on you. He'd suggest an honest question: what in this desire is about the particular person, and what is about what you yourself are missing in your own life?
forbidden_attraction.practice: Consider two questions in turn, taking a slow breath between them: “What draws me to this person?” and “What's missing in my life?” Just look at whether there's a connection between the answers.

social_anxiety.text: Shy, stooped, with uneven trouser legs, Kierkegaard went out every day into Copenhagen's busy streets — and considered these walks part of his work. Fear of other people's judgment turns a simple meeting into an exam, and it's exhausting. Kierkegaard offered an unusual image in Purity of Heart Is to Will One Thing. We're used to thinking that we stand on a stage and the people around us are the audience. He turns this picture around: each person is the actor, and there is only one true spectator — the one before whom a person answers for their life. For Kierkegaard this is God; but even in a secular reading the meaning remains: the main question isn't “how do I look in the eyes of the crowd?” but “was I myself just now?” Seen this way, nervousness doesn't make you worse, and the judgment of every passing glance stops being final. The spectator who really matters looks not at your polish but at your honesty.
social_anxiety.practice: After a nerve-racking meeting, ask yourself not “how did I come across?” but “where was I myself today?” Name at least one such moment aloud.

uncertainty.text: “Life can only be understood backwards, but it must be lived forwards,” Kierkegaard wrote in his journal. Uncertainty is tiring: you want to know what will happen, and you can't. In his discourses on the lilies of the field and the birds of the air, Kierkegaard made a subtle observation. The bird doesn't worry about tomorrow — not because it's wiser, but because it has no tomorrow. A human being, though, can imagine tomorrow — and this is both our greatness and the source of our worries. In this light, your anxiety about the unknown is the flip side of a very human ability to see ahead. Kierkegaard didn't suggest giving it up. He suggested learning one thing from the bird: to live today so fully that tomorrow doesn't take it away entirely. The future remains unknown, but you still have “today” — the only time in which you can act.
uncertainty.practice: Choose one task that belongs only to today and do it completely, like Kierkegaard's bird that has no “tomorrow.” Leave tomorrow's things to tomorrow.

waiting.text: In the spring of 1843, in church, Regine Olsen nodded to Kierkegaard — and for a long time he lived on that nod, waiting to see what would come next. Waiting for an answer, results or news stretches time out, and it's hard to find your place in it. Kierkegaard wrote one of his early upbuilding discourses on “To Gain One's Soul in Patience.” His thought is unexpected: patience doesn't just help you get through the waiting — in it, a person gains themselves. When we can't speed anything up, all that remains is how we relate to the waiting, and it's precisely here that the self becomes visible. So the time of waiting isn't an empty gap but time that also belongs to your life. Kierkegaard didn't demand serenity. The nervousness will stay, but you can ask yourself: who do I want to be while I wait? This question gives back to you some of what waiting seems to take away.
waiting.practice: Sit comfortably and for ten breaths simply wait, speeding nothing up. On each out-breath ask yourself, “Who do I want to be while I wait?” Kierkegaard would call it gaining your soul in patience.

regret.text: Kierkegaard never found out whether he had been right to break off his engagement — and he kept coming back to that decision all his life. Regret can be very persistent — about what you did and what you didn't. In Either/Or, through the mouth of his aesthete hero, Kierkegaard ironically showed that regret lies in wait whatever you choose: marry, and you'll regret it; don't marry, and you'll regret that too. It sounds bleak, but it lifts part of the burden: there never was a path free of regret. And in the second part of the book, Judge William proposes a different answer — to choose yourself wholly, including your past. For Kierkegaard, a person who accepts their history neither erases it nor punishes themselves for it, but acknowledges: this is me too, and I go on with it. It follows that regret isn't a verdict but part of the material from which you keep becoming yourself.
regret.practice: Say aloud, “This, too, is part of my story, and from it I know that…” — and finish it. Judge William would call it choosing yourself together with your past.

quote.text: Marry, and you will regret it; do not marry, and you will also regret it; marry or do not marry, you will regret it either way.
quote.author: Søren Kierkegaard

longing.text: When he met Regine, by then married, on the streets of Copenhagen, Kierkegaard never spoke to her — and, it is said, planned his walks so as to glimpse her even from afar. When you miss one particular person, it pulls you back toward what was. In Repetition, Kierkegaard distinguished two ways of being connected with what has been lost: recollection and repetition. Recollection looks back and keeps the past as it was; repetition is the same movement, but forward: what was dear can become alive again in the present, even if in a new form. In Either/Or he described “the unhappiest one” — a person who lives only in recollection and is therefore absent from their own life. In other words, you don't need to drive your longing away: it speaks of love. But you can ask what of what this person gave you can live in you now too — in a habit, a word, a way of seeing the world.
longing.practice: Name one thing you took on from this person or lived through with them. Do something in its spirit today — Kierkegaard would call it repetition rather than recollection.

quote.text: Repetition and recollection are the same movement, except in opposite directions.
quote.author: Søren Kierkegaard

world_pain.text: 1848: revolutions across Europe, a war in Denmark itself — and Kierkegaard is writing about “the neighbor” and “the single individual.” Pain for the world can grow to a size you can't live with. Kierkegaard almost always thought about the single individual, and this helps here in an unexpected way. In Works of Love he insisted that love is directed not at humanity in general but at the “neighbor” — the concrete person next to you. Think this through, and pain for the whole world at once is almost unbearable, because “the world” is an abstraction, and you are a concrete person. Compassion doesn't have to embrace everything. It becomes real when it finds one face, one task, one act. Your sensitivity isn't a mistake. But you can carry it on a human scale — the scale of the neighbor, not the whole planet.
world_pain.practice: Name one specific person — near or far — whom you can help today or simply give some attention to, and do it. Kierkegaard would say this is how compassion finds its face.

rejection.text: Mocked books, indifferent professors, Bishop Mynster who never took him seriously — Kierkegaard was turned away more than once. Rejection hurts, and the pain isn't exaggerated. In The Sickness unto Death, Kierkegaard gives the example of a girl who has lost her beloved. He notes that she despairs not only over him but over herself — over the self she wanted to gain in his love, which now seems unbearable to her. Then rejection wounds so deeply because we invest our self in someone else's choice. Kierkegaard didn't deny this pain. But his answer is that the self can't be grounded in another person's decision: it is rooted deeper — in your own relationship to yourself. A refusal takes away the hope of a particular future, but it can't take you away from yourself.
rejection.practice: Say aloud, “With this person, I hoped to become…” — and finish it. Then name which of this you can become without them: your self, Kierkegaard would say, is rooted deeper than someone else's choice.

abandonment.text: How do you live with what could happen but hasn't yet? This is the central question of Kierkegaard's The Concept of Anxiety. The fear of being abandoned can be an almost constant background, and that is very hard. There he wrote that anxiety, unlike fear, is directed not at a concrete threat but at possibility — at what could happen. That's why it's so hard to calm with arguments: everything is fine right now, but the possibility of loss remains. Kierkegaard, unexpectedly, saw anxiety as a teacher. He believed that anxiety, if you don't run from it, teaches us our freedom and our bond with what is dear to us. This means your fear isn't a weakness but a sign of how much the people close to you mean to you. There's no need to be ashamed of it. You can learn to live with it: notice it, name it, and not let it alone decide what is true.
abandonment.practice: When the fear rises, name it aloud the way Kierkegaard drew the distinction: “This is fear of a possibility, not a fact.” Then touch one thing that is really here beside you right now.

quote.text: Whoever has learned to be anxious in the right way has learned the ultimate.
quote.author: Søren Kierkegaard
quote.source: The Concept of Anxiety, ch. V (1844)

unrequited.text: A young man in love with a princess — this is one of Kierkegaard's tenderest parables, written by a man who had himself given up the woman he loved. Love without an answer is one of the loneliest pains. In Fear and Trembling, Kierkegaard told a parable about a young man in love with a princess who is beyond his reach. The young man doesn't renounce his love or try to forget it by pretending it was foolishness. He makes what Kierkegaard called “infinite resignation”: he gives up the claim to its fulfillment but keeps the love itself as part of his life. Kierkegaard writes that such love remains eternally young in him. In Kierkegaard's terms, your love wasn't a mistake, and it doesn't have to disappear for you to go on living. You can let go of expecting an answer without betraying what you felt. It's a hard movement, and it takes time.
unrequited.practice: Tell yourself aloud, “I can keep this love without expecting an answer.” Kierkegaard would call it infinite resignation — notice what responds in you as you say it.

humiliation.text: Kierkegaard himself challenged a satirical paper to a fight — and lost: for a whole year the entire city laughed at him. Humiliation wounds deeply, and he knew it from his own experience. In 1846 the satirical paper The Corsair began mocking him: it drew caricatures, ridiculed his gait and even his uneven trouser legs. On the streets of Copenhagen, boys laughed at him. Kierkegaard took it hard, but it was precisely then that he formulated especially clearly the idea of “the single individual” — the separate person who doesn't dissolve into the crowd's judgment. As he understood it, the laughter of the public can't determine who a person really is. Seen this way, your pain is real, but humiliation is what others did to you, not what you have become. The dignity of the self lies deeper than anyone's mockery can reach.
humiliation.practice: Walk slowly, with a straight back, the way Kierkegaard kept walking the streets where people laughed at him. With each step, silently name one thing in you that remains untouched.

body_shame.text: Stooped, with a crooked back and thin legs, Kierkegaard was a favourite target for caricaturists. If your own body has seemed wrong to you for years, it is a heavy burden. In The Concept of Anxiety Kierkegaard wrote that a human being is a synthesis of soul and body, united by spirit — that is, by a living relationship to oneself. The body here isn't an appendage or a mistake but part of who you are. In The Sickness unto Death he described a despair in which a person doesn't want to be themselves and dreams of becoming someone else, as if changing clothes. In this light, shame about your body can be one form of this unwillingness — a refusal of your “necessity,” of what is given and not chosen. Kierkegaard saw the way out not in loving everything at once, but in consenting to be yourself, this person, in this body — and moving on from there.
body_shame.practice: Put your palm on your chest and say silently, “This is my body, and I am it too.” Don't evaluate; just feel the warmth of your palm and the breath beneath it.

illness.text: What stays yours when the body no longer obeys? Kierkegaard didn't ask this in the abstract. When your body lets you down, the world narrows, and this can be enraging, frightening and exhausting. Kierkegaard was in fragile health all his life, and in his journals he wrote of his “thorn in the flesh” — the apostle Paul's phrase for a suffering that doesn't go away. He devoted one of his upbuilding discourses to this image. Kierkegaard didn't pretend that such a thorn was good or useful. But his philosophy suggests that the self isn't only a body but a relation that relates itself to itself. Illness limits you, but the way you relate to it, and to yourself within it, remains yours. So you don't have to demand heroism of yourself or pretend to be well. It's enough to remain yourself within what is possible today.
illness.practice: Say, “Even now I remain a person who…” — and name one trait the illness hasn't taken away. Repeat the sentence once more, more slowly.

pride.text: Kierkegaard wanted just two words on his gravestone: “That Individual.” Pride in what you've done is a joyful, well-earned feeling. Kierkegaard invited us to see in it what makes it truly healthy. For him, a person's main task was to become themselves — that is, not simply to get a result, but to choose and carry out something as their own act. Judge William in Either/Or describes the ethical life as a life in which a person answers for what they do. It follows that the best pride isn't superiority over others but joy that you really acted and became a little more yourself. Such pride doesn't need comparing and doesn't need hiding. You can simply live it as a moment when the self coincides with its deed.
pride.practice: Sit in silence for a minute and recall one choice you made on the way to this result. Tell yourself, “That was my decision,” and notice what it's like to coincide with your deed.

melancholy.text: Kierkegaard wrote in his journal that he had been in the grip of a deep melancholy since childhood and had learned to hide it behind cheerfulness. Gentle sadness is a quiet state in which sorrow feels almost like kin. Kierkegaard knew it as few others did: all his life he called himself a melancholic, and in the “Diapsalmata” of Either/Or his aesthete speaks of his sorrow as a secure refuge. Kierkegaard saw in melancholy depth and sensitivity, an ability to hear what gets lost in the bustle. But in the second part of the same book, Judge William gently objects: melancholy can become a place where a person hides from choice. Both voices are valuable. In other words, you can let yourself stay in this sadness without hurrying to chase it away — and notice whether it's calling you toward something. Melancholy can be both a home and a door.
melancholy.practice: Write your melancholy a short letter under a pseudonym — as Kierkegaard would — and ask it, “What are you about?” The answer can be a single word.

quote.text: My grief is my baronial castle.
quote.author: Søren Kierkegaard
